newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives in no mood for time in opposition.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives in no mood for time in opposition.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives may be way behind in the opinion polls, split over Europe and facing a rejuvenated Labour party, but party activists are in no mood for a term in opposition.

Rank and file Conservatives said on Thursday they did not want to see any last minute gimmicks to claw back support. If the government sticks to its current policies, they say, it can still win the election now no more than seven months away.

"The government just has to keep doing what is has been doing," said Elaine Byrom, chairman of Bradford West constituency party. "People will vote on what they have in their pocket, and that's more than they had at the last election."

Like the bulk of party members, she dismissed the current showing in the polls, harking back to the 1992 election when polls wrongly forecast a narrow Labour victory. "The polls are wrong. I can see that from campaigning on the doorstep."
And many activists do not want to see Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke make big tax cuts in the November budget, the last before the general election.
"We are hoping to see tax cuts, but not cuts we can't afford," said Derek Duval, a party representative at the conference. "We are conservatives and that means sensible policies first and foremost."
Clarke has been rounded on by the party's rightwingers in recent weeks for deflating expectations of budget tax cuts.
But at Bournemouth there was little other than praise for the Chancellor's economic policies.
The economy is in its fifth year of growth and, according to Clarke, is the envy of the world with its commendable combination of a steady pickup in activity and low inflation.
On his views on Europe, however, it was a different story.
"I have nothing against Clarke's handling of the economy, but I don't trust him on Europe," said Brian Rathbone, another local party representative.
Rathbone is worried Clarke, eager to meet tough criteria on fiscal deficits Britain must reach if it is to enter a European single currency, will grant only marginal tax cuts in November.
"There is nothing wrong with the Maastricht criteria in themselves. They are very good and laudable. But I don't like Clarke's position on economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Clarke is just delaying the decision on EMU for as long as possible in the hope that it just builds up a head of steam and we get dragged in. I want to see John Major rule it out before the election. Then we'll win it (the election) hands down."
But while calls for a harder line on Europe have captured headlines, many rank-and-file Tories still support the government's present wait-and-see policy.
Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind won a surprise standing ovation on Wednesday when he said to force a decision on a single currency now would not impress voters.
"Conference audiences don't often warm to Mr Rifkind but... he really gave us something to unite around on Wednesday," said Paul Short, from the inner London area of Holborn.
With the opposition Labour party well ahead in opinion polls, party strategists are just hoping this unity will last until the election to give them a chance to fight back.
